title: Deoptimization
concept: Code that breaks the engine's assumptions triggers 'deoptimization (Deopt)', degrading performance.

steps.title: Defining the add function
steps.explanation:
Defining the `add` function.
At this point, it can accept any type.
steps.keyInsight: JavaScript functions have no type information. Any type can come in at runtime.

steps.title: Creating the results array
steps.explanation:
Creating the `results` array.
It will store the results of function calls.

steps.title: First numeric addition
steps.explanation: `add(1, 2)` = 3. The engine starts learning: "Ah, this function takes numbers."
steps.keyInsight: V8 observes function call patterns and 'profiles' them.

steps.title: Second numeric addition
steps.explanation:
`add(3, 4)` = 7. Numbers again! The engine's confidence grows.
"This function is for numbers!"
steps.keyInsight: When called with the same type repeatedly, the engine decides to 'optimize'.

steps.title: Third numeric addition + optimization
steps.explanation: `add(5, 6)` = 11. The pattern is confirmed — V8 generates optimized machine code.
steps.keyInsight: The JIT compiler creates machine code specialized for number addition. No type checks — straight to addition!
steps.analogy: Like ordering 'the usual' at your favorite restaurant — it comes out fast because they know exactly what you want.

steps.title: Saving the optimized state
steps.explanation:
Copying the results so far [3, 7, 11] into `optimized`.
At this point, the function is in an optimized state.

steps.title: Type change — Deoptimization!
steps.explanation:
`add('Hello', 'World')` = 'HelloWorld'.
Strings suddenly arrived! The engine's prediction is shattered.
steps.keyInsight: When the type changes, the optimized machine code is discarded and execution falls back to interpreter mode (Bailout).
steps.analogy: Like walking into your favorite restaurant and ordering something not on the menu — it takes much longer.

memoryState.reason: Type mismatch: expected Number, got String

steps.title: Saving state after Deopt
steps.explanation:
Saving the post-deoptimization results into `afterDeopt`.
The results are still correct, but performance has taken a hit.
steps.keyInsight: Functionally correct, but the same function is now slower.

steps.title: Comparing results
steps.explanation:
optimized = [3, 7, 11], afterDeopt = [3, 7, 11, 'HelloWorld'].
The string result is correct, but there's a hidden performance cost internally.
steps.keyInsight: Deopt is invisible in the output but impacts performance. You can see it in the DevTools Performance tab.

quiz.question: How do you keep the JIT compiler's optimizations in place?
options: Use as many different types as possible in variables
quiz.explanation:
V8 is fastest when a function always receives the same argument types (Monomorphic).
Alternating between numbers, strings, and objects (Polymorphic) causes V8 to give up on optimization.

misconceptions.correct: It compiles in real-time at runtime (JIT).
misconceptions.why: The JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler translates code to machine code at runtime, so for consistent patterns it can reach performance comparable to statically typed languages like C++ and Java.

misconceptions.wrong: Results are fine as long as they're correct, even if types change
misconceptions.correct: The results are correct, but performance degrades.
misconceptions.why:
The engine discards the optimized code and falls back to the slower interpreter mode.
For performance-critical code, type consistency matters a lot.

keyTakeaway: Don't change a function's input types (Signature). Keeping the engine's assumptions intact is the core of performance optimization.
